chunks.content: 96 How to make sure you get a good deal when buying or selling and accounting practice The Stages of a Deal: A Step-by-Step Guide From Sara Sharp: Navigating the Process of Buying an Accounting Firm Hi Everyone, I’m Sara Sharp, and I help people buy and sell accounting firms. Buying a firm can seem like a daunting process, but if you break it down into clear steps, it’s much easier to manage. Here’s a simple guide to help you understand each stage of the deal-making process. 1. Determining Your Deal Box Before you start looking for a firm to buy, you need to define your “deal box.” This means figuring out what kind of firm you’re looking for. Consider the size, location, client base, and services offered. Knowing exactly what you want will help you focus your search. Location Asking Price Types of Clients Services Offered Firm Size by Revenue or Employee Count Sellers Discretionary Earnings aka Cashflow 2. Searching Online Marketplaces Once you know what you’re looking for, start searching online marketplaces. There are many websites that specialize in listing accounting practices for sale. You can filter the search results to match your deal box criteria, ie List Price, Revenue, Cashflow, Location, etc. Examples: BizBuySell.com Accountingpracticeexchange.com 3. Submitting an NDA, Personal Financial Statement, and Resume When you find a firm that fits, the next step is to submit a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). The NDA ensures that all information shared between you and the seller remains confidential. Pair the NDA with a Personal Financial Statement (PFS). The Personal Financial Statement shows the seller that you have the financial ability to buy the firm. It may include proof of funds or an SBA Pre-Qualification letter. Attach your resume. This outlines your experience and qualifications to show the seller you're prepared to run the firm. SBA Personal Financial Statement 4. Seller Meeting If the seller is interested in moving forward, you’ll have a meeting to discuss the firm in more detail. First impressions are EVERYTHING. So take great care with this call. This is your chance to ask questions, learn more about the business, and see if it’s a good fit for you. But most importantly, remember this firm is their baby. Don’t call their baby ugly the first time you meet. It’s an opportunity to build rapport with the seller, which will be essential as you move forward. 5. Submitting an LOI (Letter of Intent) After the seller meeting, if you decide you want to buy the firm, you’ll submit a Letter of Intent (LOI). The LOI outlines the basic terms of the deal, such as the purchase price, payment terms, and any conditions that need to be met. It’s not legally binding, but it shows the seller that you’re serious about moving forward. Become an LOI Expert here 6. Due Diligence Once the LOI is signed, the due diligence process begins. This is where you carefully review all aspects of the business. This includes financial statements, client contracts, and operations. Due diligence helps you confirm that the business is as it was represented and identify any potential risks. Sample Due Diligence Document Request List: Last 3 years Income Statements Last 3 years Tax Returns Current Balance Sheet AR Aging Summary Bank Statements General Ledger Employee List Vendor List Client List Contracts Consider hiring a CPA who specializes in due diligence to perform a Quality of Earnings assessment. 7. Securing Funding While in due diligence, you’ll want to start the process to secure funding for the deal. This could involve getting a loan from a bank, finding investors, or using your own savings. It’s important to have your financing in place before you move on to the final steps. If you plan to apply for an SBA 7(a) loan, make sure you’re working with an SBA Preferred Lender. That can save you months in processing time! 8. Closing the Deal After securing funding, you’re ready to close the deal. This is where all the final paperwork is signed, and the business officially changes hands. Closing the deal usually involves working with attorneys to ensure everything is done correctly. 9. Transitioning Ownership Finally, after the deal closes, you’ll need to transition ownership. This includes training from the previous owner. Introducing yourself to clients and employees. Making necessary changes to the business operations. A smooth transition is key to maintaining the firm’s success and keeping clients and staff happy. Buying an accounting firm isn't easy. But follow these stages, and you can navigate the process with confidence. Remember, each step is important. Take your time to get things right. It will pay off in the long run. If you ever have any questions or need guidance, I’m here to help you through each stage of the deal. I hope this guide helps you feel more prepared for your next big move.
